timeline_list.title: Sound Comes to Universal Horror
timeline_list.description: Robert Julian (1879-1943) and John Willard (1885-1942) direct The Cat Creeps (1930), Universal's first sound horror film.

timeline_list.title: The Beginning of Gangsters on Screen
timeline_list.description: Roadhouse Nights, starring Jimmy Durante (1893-1980), is the first of many gangster films inspired by Dashiell Hammett's novel Red Harvest (1929).

timeline_list.title: Stop-motion
timeline_list.description: Le roman de renard (The Tale of the Fox, 1930), by Wladyslaw Starevich (1882-1965), is one of the greatest achievements in stop-motion animation.

timeline_list.title: A Template
timeline_list.description: Little Caesar sets the template for future gangster films and introduces a new vocabulary: gats (guns), molls (girls) and bulls (cops).

timeline_list.title: War at the Oscars
timeline_list.description: All Quiet on the Western Front (1930), by Lewis Milestone (1895-1980), wins the Oscar for Best Picture.

timeline_list.title: Defying a Revolution
timeline_list.description: Chaplin releases the classic City Lights (1931), defying the talkie revolution. It was one of the last silent films produced in the United States, along with F. W. Murnau's Tabu (1931), shot in Polynesia.

timeline_list.title: Gothic Horror
timeline_list.description: Dracula and Frankenstein are released. They unleash a flood of Gothic horror films seeking to repeat their commercial success.

timeline_list.title: Peludopolis
timeline_list.description: Quirino Cristiani, one of the forgotten giants of animation, makes Peludo City, the first animated feature film to use synchronized sound.

timeline_list.title: Freaks
timeline_list.description: Freaks is released by MGM. The film sparks a series of controversies and cuts short the career of its director, Tod Browning.

timeline_list.title: Laurel and Hardy
timeline_list.description: Laurel and Hardy's The Music Box wins the first Oscar for Best Short Subject (comedy).

timeline_list.title: Betty Boop
timeline_list.description: In Betty Boop's Bamboo Isle (1932), the title character displays her trademark wide-eyed promiscuity.

timeline_list.title: Stop-Motion and King Kong
timeline_list.description: The use of stop-motion takes an enormous evolutionary leap with the release of the fantasy film King Kong.

timeline_list.title: Consequences of Nazism
timeline_list.description: Hitler comes to power in Germany, triggering an exodus of German creative talent to Hollywood, London and Paris.

timeline_list.title: The Musical Revitalized
timeline_list.description: Warner Bros. makes 42nd Street and Gold Diggers of 1933. They revitalize the musical genre and become two of the year's biggest box office hits.

timeline_list.title: The Three Stooges
timeline_list.description: Woman Haters, the first feature film starring The Three Stooges, is released.

timeline_list.title: Bride of Frankenstein
timeline_list.description: Bride of Frankenstein, by James Whale, is the first sequel to the original film and features a female monster. It is considered better than its predecessor.

timeline_list.title: A Child Star
timeline_list.description: Child star Shirley Temple receives a special Oscar at the age of 7. Temple was Hollywood's highest-grossing child actress at the box office.

timeline_list.title: Resisting Sound
timeline_list.description: Almost 10 years after the first talking picture, Chaplin releases Modern Times (1936), his first "sound" film. With no dialogue, it contains only sound effects.

timeline_list.title: Top Hat
timeline_list.description: Top Hat receives four Oscar nominations, including Best Picture and Best Dance Direction.

timeline_list.title: Frank Capra
timeline_list.description: Frank Capra wins his second Oscar for directing Mr. Deeds Goes to Town.

timeline_list.title: Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers
timeline_list.description: Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers star in Swing Time, one of the best of their 10 on-screen partnerships.

timeline_list.title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
timeline_list.description: Disney's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs is released.

timeline_list.title: Bringing Up Baby
timeline_list.description: Bringing Up Baby, by Howard Hawks, is a box office flop, but over the years it becomes a beloved classic of the genre.

timeline_list.title: Rebellion
timeline_list.description: William Wyler's (1902-1981) urban gangster film Dead End introduces The Dead End Kids, possibly cinema's first gang of rebellious teenagers.

timeline_list.title: The Magic of Technicolor
timeline_list.description: The Wizard of Oz (1939) is released in theaters, instantly becoming a classic and enchanting children and adults alike. But with its release, audiences also witnessed the power of Technicolor in storytelling, as when Dorothy leaves her sepia world for the colorful world of Oz. What the visionary Natalie Kalmus had envisioned was becoming reality.

timeline_list.title: Anti-Nazism in Hollywood
timeline_list.description: Confessions of a Nazi Spy (1939), about the real-life trial of a spy, is the first explicitly anti-Nazi film made in Hollywood.

timeline_list.title: The Resurgence of the Western
timeline_list.description: Stagecoach (1939), Jesse James (1939), Dodge City (1939) and Destry Rides Again (1939) kick off the resurgence of the Western.
